BOARD OF EDUCATION.
An important meeting of the board of education was held last evening at which the corps of janitors was filled and other routine business disposed of preparatory to the opening of the fall term of school the week of September 12.

The following panitors were elected: Central building, James Workman; West school, T. F. Dow; East school, George Stout, and Glenover school, J. W. Jackson.

The resignation of Miss Mollie Moore as principal of the West school was received and accepted. Miss Starr of Pawnee City is an applicant for the position and will probably be selected to fill the vacancy.

The course of study for the ensuing year in the high school has been rearranged by the board with the assistance of Superintendent E. J. Bodwell and Principal N. M. Souder. The change is made necessary by reason of the addition of the domestic science and manual training departments to the regular course of study. Apparatus for both departments are now being installed and will be ready for use the opening day of school.

The improvements at Central building are rapidly nearing completion. The building is being put in

almost perfect sanitary condition ad the change to the stairway will be appreciated by all students attending this school. Aside from the improvements at the Central building toilet rooms are being installed in the East and Fairview schools and the oil which has so long disfigured the flors in all of the schools is being scoured off.

Miss Marian Reed was last evening appointed supervisor of drawing.

POPULATION DECREASING.

The two negroes arrested Sunday by the local officers, one of them being charged with vagrancy and the other with soliciting for a disorderly house, were given a hearing in police court before Judge Ellis late yesterday afternoon. The first was given ten days in jail and the other was fined $25 and costs. Last evening two more negroes, a man and a woman were arrested by Officers Clyde Reed and Hy Bales.

The four, with a number of their friends, eight in all, were ordered out of town by the police and they took the early morning Burlington for Lincoln. Within the past few days a number of very undesirable characters have landed in Beatrice from the capitol city and in the future they will be ordered to make themselves scarce and keep out of the corporate limits of Beatrice.

Fremont.—That George Osborne's confession that he murdered John Hoctoor because the itinerant eye-glass peddler had insulted him is true only with regard to the statement that he committed the crime, is the belief of County Attorney Cook and Sheriff Bauman, who have been studying the case. They believe that the motive was robbery, and a charge of first degree murder may be filed against the prisoner. Osborne made the confession basing his cause for killing Hoctor on a statement that the peddler had insulted him.

To Censor Advertising.

Beatrice.—An agreement has been adopted by which the merchants of this place consent to refuse to patronize all such advertising schemes as hotel registers, cook books, race track programs, society or church programs and newspaper schemes presented by traveling promoters or agents. A committee will censor all schemes presented to the merchants and without the approval of this committee no patronage will be given.

Will Hold Reunion.

Dakota City.—Arrangements have been completed for the twenty-ninth annual reunion of the Pioneers and Old Settlers' association of Dakota county. The reunion will be held at Clinton park, Dakota City, August 25. John A. Ehrhardt of Stanton will be the principal speaker. The attendance at these reunions has always been large, ranging from 5,000 to 12,000 persons.

To Have Library Building.

Alliance. At a recent meeting of the Alliance library board the contract for architectural work on the proposed building was let to a Black Hills firm. The building will be 40x50 feet, one story and basement. The material used for the basement will be cut stone. The balance of the building will be of gray pressed brick.

One thousand red "Ask Me" buttons have been secured by the Lincoln Commercial club to be worn by members of committees during the state fair.

The new rectory in St. Anthony's parish at St. Charles, a wealthy settlement of Germans near West Point, was dedicated with appropriate ceremonies.

George Green, a Burlington fireman, lost a leg at Mapps siding, near York. In some manner unexplained he fell from the engine and the wheels ran over his leg.

Attempting to cross the tracks in the Burlington yards under the Tenth street viaduct at Omaha, an unidentified man was struck by a Union Pacific engine Thursday morning, and instantly killed.

Burglaries entered through the cellar window of Aufdengarten's store at Ashland and, finding the safe unlocked, abstracted the cash drawer, containing $100. The empty drawer was found later.

The twenty-sixth annual fair of the Boone County Agricultural association, will be held at Albion on September 20 to 23, inclusive. Among the other attractions will be exhibitions and contests in riding bucking bronchos, roping and tying steers and cowboy sports.

The committee having the house warming and dedication of the new Burlington shop buildings at Havelock in charge has chosen Saturday, September 3, as the date of the festivities. Prominent speakers are being engaged and light refreshments will be served.

Owing to the installation of domestic science and manual training departments in the high school, the board of education has found it necessary to rearrange the course of study at Beatrice. School begins September 12, a week later than usual, to permit the students to attend the state fair.

Several of the families who left Stromsburg in the spring to take up homesteads in Montana have returned. They say it was nearly impossible to get water there even for drinking purposes and the cattle and horses had to drink from ponds.

The Swedish Lutheran church of Osceola was struck by lightning during a storm. The roof caught fire and considerable damage resulted to the interior decorations.

A result of recent gospel test meetings will probably be the organization of an Adventist church in York.

Mrs. Carrie Nation delivered one of her characteristic lectures at the Albion Chautauqua last week.

The Tecumseh Chautauqua just ceased is said to have been one of the most successful in that part of the state.

While swimming in the Platte river at Wahoo, Carl Thorson of Mead became lodged in a suck hole and was drowned.

A four-year-old boy at Beatrice, who walked in his sleep, got almost a block from home before waking one night last week.

An itinerant peddler believed to be John Hoctor of Iowa was murdered in the Northwestern railroad yards at Fremont, probably by tramps.

Raccoons have become so plentiful on the Blue river near Hastings that they have become a menace to the farmers. Hen roosts are nightly raided.

Rev. Father Vogleman, who has been in charge of St. Joseph's Catholic church at Beatrice for the last few months, has gone to Nebraska City, where he will take charge of a parish.

Will Mathorn was instantly killed at Blair Friday by a live electric light wire. He was at the top of a pole trying to disconnect a transformer when he accidentally came in contact with two wires carrying 1,100 volts.

The Beatrice coursing club is considering the matter of holding a meeting on Thanksgiving. About seventy-five grey hounds are owned in that vicinity and it is believed that with liberal purses offered, a successful meeting can be pulled off.

Fire caused a loss of between $30,000 and $35,000 to the Griswold Seed company at Lincoln. Their elevator and warehouse was more than half consumed and the stock contained said to be a total loss. The stock was estimated between $20,000 and $30,000 and the building at about $6,000. The loss was fully covered by insurance.

A number of negroes who have been in Beatrice the past few days have been ordered out of town. Three colored men were arrested, charged with vagrancy and one colored woman was charged with disorderly conduct. The city authorities will endeavor to keep characters of this class out of the city in the future.

A vender in razors who was operating his business at the Beaver Crossing picnic had his prosperity turned to adversity when the constable took him in charge and landed him in the county jail. The price of his wares was one dollar and the purchasers were handed razors instead of any change that might be coming to them. One man being twenty razors richer after doing business with him.

The reservation of the grand stand is to be tried for the first time at the Nebraska state fair this year. Another innovation is the offering for sale of season tickets good at the outside gates, $2. For two dollars one can go to the fair daily for six days. A collection of living cactuses from Arizona was received by the State university recently which will be grown in the greenhouse. What is considered particularly valuable in this collection is a small specimen of the giant cactus which grows to a height of from thirty to forty feet in its native country. Dr. C. E. Bessey is wondering what he will do when the baby cactus grows up and becomes too large for its present quarters and he is planning an upward extension of one end of the greenhouse.

Assistant Attorney General George Ayers has returned from North Platte where he obtained a dissolution of the injunctions issued by the county judge of Scotts Bluff county. NEGRO SHOOTS UP TOWN.
Narrow Escape From a Lynching at Dover, Del.
DOVER, Del., July 31. The State capital of Delaware would have been the scene of a lynching had not two sturdy policemen got Joseph Tough Turner around to a safe place after Turner, following a new custom of some angry Delaware negroes, had emptied his 32 calibre revolver in crowded Loockerman street, Dover's busiest thoroughfare.

Turner got into an altercation with another negro and before he had exhausted his bullets he had, risking the lives of scores of citizens, shot two negroes, one an old man.

Turner has been in many shooting altercations, but none quite so desperate as to-day's.

HOLD MAN ON
SHOOTING CHARGE
Special to THE EVENING JOURNAL. DOVER, Del., Aug. 1.—Lewis W. Davis, the negro who is accused of having done most of the gun play on Loockerman street Saturday night in which Joseph "Tough" Turner, was also engaged and was shot, has been held by Magistrate Wood to await the result of Turner's injuries. This was the shooting affray that almost ended in a lynching when the Saturday night crowd realized how many lives had been risked in the negroes altercation.

CRY "LYNCH" IN DOVER STREETS
DOVER, Del., Aug. 1.—A crowd threatened to lynch Joseph Turner, a negro, after he had emptied his revolver on Lockerman street, the capital's busiest thoroughfae, wounded two other negroes and endangered the lives of many citizens. Turner had been in several shooting affrays, but none as serious as that of to-day. During the excitement of the shooting and arrest men dashed toward Turner, calling to each other to "get a rope." Policemen, seized the negro and hurried him to jail.

DOVER NEGRO WOUNDED IN A SHOOTING AFFRAY
Joseph Turner, colored, aged 30 years, whose home is in Dover, is in a critical condition at the Delaware Hospital in Wilmington with two bullet wounds in his back and another in his abdomen. Turner and some other negroes were in a crowd near Dover on Saturday morning, when a fight started, during which it is alleged Turner struck Lewis Davis on the head with a whiskey bottle and inflicted an ugly wound. Turner escaped and Lewis went home and armed himself with a revolver, after which he started out to look for Turner. He found Turner Saturday evening, and without warning opened fire. Turner turned and ran away. The man fired five shots at him, but only two of them took effect. One bullet is believed to have passed through Turner's back and gone into his stomach and his condition as a result is thought to be very critical. Turner was unable to tell any particulars about the case or to give the name of his assailant. His sister, who went to Wilmington with him, told the facts. Davis has been held by Magistrate Wood to await the result of the injuries to Turner.

SIX PRISONERS OVERPOWERED
THE SHERIFF ON WEDNESDAY
The Escape Was For Short Time For a Possee Quickly Rounded Them Up.—Big Jail Delivery Planned
maloney is congratulating himself on the narrow escape he had yesterday when a jail delivery was made, as he has ascertained that the plot laid by the desperadoes was to call him to the door, when the umbrella mender, George Stout, was released, seize him, take the keys and make a general delivery. This information was told the sheriff last evening by one of the trusties at the jail who knew of the plot and had been asked to join in the escape. Sheriff Maloney is grateful to the citizens of Dover who aided in the capture of the prisoners and their recovery within one hour after the delivery was made. The sheriff, who had been out of town all the morning, arrived home about 11.30 o'clock and when informed that George Stout, the umbrella mender, who had been serving a 10 days' sentence for drnkenness, desired to be released, his time havng expired, before handing in the dinner, which was also ready, he went to the prison door and opened it for Stout to come out. Instead of passing out he pushed the sheriff against the iron door, allowing it to swing open full, thus giving the other prisoners, who were out in the corridor, the chance to rush by the sheriff. Sheriff Maloney tried to push Stout back, but before he could do it, Fred Jacobs, a negro, struck him on the head, but not hard enough to knock him out. He was slightly stunned and as he staggered back Leander Deshields grabbed him and endeavored to hold him while the other prisoners made their escape. Fearing, however, that he might be captured, Deshields released the sheriff and made a break himself. Of the six prisoners escaping, three were white and three were black. The three white men being Lewis Brickner, awaiting trial for defrauding; Leander Deshie ds, for highway robbery and attempted murder, and William Jackson, for carrying concealed a deadly weapon. The negroes were Lewis Davis, awaiting trial for the attempted murder of "Tough" Turner; Frederick Jacobs, attempted murder, and Ernest Plummer, assault and battery. When the men left the jail they separated, Brickner, Jackson and Plummer running through a cornfield back of the State House, while the others ran toward St. Jones' River. The second trio were the first ones apprehended, Deshields and Jacobs being caught by Dr. W. D. Burton, deputy clerk of the peace who saw them as they were swimming across the creek. Dr. Burton, levelled his double-barreled gun at them, which induced both to return without much persuasion. Davis hid in a hog pen on the farm adjoining the creek and was apprehended by Charles Wilson, the tenant, taken into custody by him and kept in his corn crib until the other two had been captured and safely landed in jail.
